changes.before: Change only the function parameter to std::span<const int>. What happens to values[0] = 9?
changes.after: Let a function view consecutive items without copying the collection.

before: std::span<T> views consecutive elements with a length. Here it borrows a std::array without copying or owning the elements. The storage must remain alive and uninvalidated while the span is used.

A span<int> permits writes to the original ints. Passing the lightweight span by value copies the view, not the array. The empty check ensures index zero exists; C++23 operator[] does not provide a mandatory bounds-checked exception.
std::span<const int> forbids changing elements through that view. const std::span<int> would instead make the view object const while leaving its int elements mutable. Neither form takes ownership.
Expected output or behavior: 9 3. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Write a read-only sum function taking span<const int> and call it with both an array and a vector. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: std::span describes a sequence of items stored next to one another in memory. It remembers their starting position and count. It does not own them, so their storage must remain alive and valid.
Passing span<int> by value copies the small view, not the array it refers to. The function can change the original integers through that view.
empty() checks whether the span has zero items. !values.empty() makes sure index zero exists before assigning to it. C++23 span's [] access does not promise a bounds-checking exception.
The program prints 9 3. setFirst changes the original first item to nine. The array still has three items.
span<const int> makes the viewed integers read-only through the span. const span<int> instead makes the view object itself const; its int elements can still be changed. The position of const matters.

before.question: Change only the function parameter to std::span<const int>. What happens to values[0] = 9?
choices: It changes the array just as before.
It creates a private copy of the array and edits that.
Compilation rejects writing through the read-only element view.
before.explanation: The viewed element type is const int, so assignment is ill-formed; no runtime attempt is needed.

after.question: Change only the parameter to std::span<const int>. What happens to values[0] = 9?
choices: It changes the original array as before.
It edits a private copy of the array.
The compiler rejects writing through the read-only element view.
after.explanation: The viewed element type is const int, so assigning a new value through the span is not allowed.
